intro: A differential equation connects a quantity to how fast it changes, like a cooling cup of coffee losing heat faster when it is hotter. This branch solves the simplest kind, which involve only the first rate of change.

VII.15.01.what: Sorting differential equations by type, since each type has its own solving method.

levels.a: Finds the order: the highest derivative (rate of change) involved.
levels.b: Tells linear equations from nonlinear ones.
levels.c: Recognizes autonomous equations, where time does not appear directly.
levels.d: Tells equations with one input variable from those with several.

VII.15.02.what: Solving linear first-order equations using an integrating factor, a clever multiplier that makes the equation easy to integrate.

levels.a: Rewrites the equation in standard form.
levels.d: Finds the one solution that matches a given starting value.

VII.15.03.what: Exact equations come from a hidden function whose level curves are the solutions.

levels.a: Tests whether an equation is exact.
levels.d: Multiplies by a factor to make a non-exact equation exact.

VII.15.04.what: Using a clever change of variable to turn a hard equation into one already known how to solve.

levels.a: Solves homogeneous equations, where the slope depends only on y divided by x.
levels.b: Solves Bernoulli equations with a standard substitution.
levels.c: Uses the substitution y equals v times x.
levels.d: Chooses the right substitution for a given equation.

VII.15.05.what: A theorem that says when an equation is guaranteed to have exactly one solution through a starting point.

levels.a: States the existence and uniqueness theorem.
levels.c: Studies an example with more than one solution.
levels.d: Finds how far a solution is guaranteed to last.

VII.15.06.what: Applying first-order equations to electrical circuits and to tanks where liquids mix.

levels.a: Solves circuits with a resistor and a capacitor.
levels.b: Solves circuits with a resistor and an inductor (coil).
levels.c: Tracks salt concentration in a tank with liquid flowing in and out.
levels.d: Interprets what happens in the long run.

VII.15.07.what: Numerical methods approximate a solution step by step when no formula can be found, as computers do.

levels.a: Uses Euler's method: repeated small steps along the current slope.
levels.b: Uses an improved version that averages two slopes.
levels.c: Uses the Runge–Kutta method, a more accurate standard.
levels.d: Compares how accurate the methods are.
